added: Lists have a third view, Planning: lay the trip out day by day and see what each day asks of you.
Drop a GPX file on a trail link and its length, climb, descent and elevation profile fill themselves in, without leaving your browser.
Give a day a distance and it works out the climb, roughly how long it will take, and roughly what it will burn.
Run your cursor along the elevation profile to read the distance, height and gradient at any point, each day in its own colour.
Set your body weight to sharpen the calorie estimates. It is never on a shared list.
The elevation profile shades how hard the ground is: red where it's steep, yellow where it's moderate.
Routes can be read from KML, TCX and GeoJSON files as well as GPX.
Map files can now be read as Google Earth KMZ and GeoRSS as well as GPX, KML, TCX and GeoJSON.
A route imported from a map file is drawn on the terrain it crosses, in the days' colours. The map never appears on a shared list.
Mark water, a camp or a landmark by tapping the map. The pin lands on that day's stretch and moves between days as the plan changes.
The map opens full screen for placing pins, with the trip's days across the top.
Each pin carries its own mark (a droplet for water, a tent for a camp), and its row names the kind.
Press and hold a pin to pick it up and slide it along the route. It re-files itself under the day it lands in.
Tap a pin on the map to name it or remove it, without hunting for its row.
Drag the tent where one day ends on the map and the two days either side trade miles.
Each day now lists where it ends (the camp) with the distance in, and you can name it.
Trace the elevation profile and a dot follows on the map, so you can see where a climb actually is.
The last day shows where the walk finishes, and you can name it the way you name a camp.
A colour key under the map names each day's colour and how far it walks.
changed: Your body weight is remembered on your device, once for every trip, and never leaves your browser.
The elevation profile's distance scale shows more marks on a wider window, and its grade always matches the shading.
A day shows its descent alongside its climb, and the trip's figures line up in columns.
The trail panel's file button now reads "Import map file" and names the formats it takes.
Gear, Packing and Planning are a labelled bar under the list's title instead of three toolbar icons. Shared lists get one too: Gear or Trip.
Hold ⌘ or Ctrl and scroll, or pinch on a trackpad, to zoom the route map.
The map opens and closes with the terrain growing out of its place on the page.
Walking times read as a range, "4–4.5 hr", since the estimate is only good to about a fifth either way.
Map pins are white drops with the mark in colour, day lines carry a darker edge, and each day's end is a camp you can drag.
The trip's time figure is labelled "Walking time": time on your feet, not the days the trip takes.
Setting what a waypoint is now takes one tap on the kind you want, the way an item's type works in Gear.
Camp is no longer something you pick. Every day's end draws one, and the pins you place are water or a landmark.
The elevation chart leaves easy ground unshaded and breaks cleanly between days.
The elevation profile now leaves a real gap between one day and the next, on the shading as well as the line.
A day's climb and its drop now sit together as one pair, and the figures after them line up down the list.
Names are tidied when you commit them: stray spaces collapse and apostrophes curl. Feet and inches are left as typed.
The route's start and finish wear a chequered flag and camps are solid dark pins, apart from the water and landmarks you place.
The map's zoom and pin-dragging instructions now sit behind a (?) instead of taking a line under the map permanently.
fixed: On a phone, a weight like 0.68 lb no longer has its last digit clipped.
A shared list no longer carries the owner's packing tick-offs in its data.
Clearing a day's distance or climb now sticks, instead of coming back the moment the list saved.
Calorie estimates were too high for heavier walkers, and a night's sleep was charged at the same rate as an evening in camp.
Waypoint rows fit a phone screen: the name on its own line, the coordinate and distance on the next.
Map pins now point exactly at the spot on the route they mark, rather than a little below it.
Routes imported before trailheads existed get their start pin, and a route's start and finish can no longer be deleted by mistake.
